extracted.intended_audience: healthcare public relations and marketing professionals (hospital, provider, medical organization, and manufacturer communications staff)
extracted.subtask_description: Practical rules and standards for creating and pitching news releases and story ideas for healthcare organizations so editors/reporters will notice and publish them. Emphasizes audience targeting, clarity, timeliness, supporting materials, and media relations etiquette.

rubrics_metrics.name: Know the publication and their audience (readers/viewers).
rubrics_metrics.description: Understand each target publication's style, tone, perspective, special requirements and deadlines by reading it before pitching.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: There is a world of difference between different publications (e.g., a local shopkeeper monthly vs. Sports Illustrated). Read the publication to understand and know their special requirements and deadlines. Editors respond when releases start with the benefit to their readers—lead with why the announcement matters to that publication's audience.

rubrics_metrics.name: Know your own audience.
rubrics_metrics.description: Identify the specific target audience for your message and write as if addressing a single representative person.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Your message should be crafted for a specific target; picture a representative individual who fits the description and write to that one person.

rubrics_metrics.name: Target the editor/reporter (gatekeeper/decision-maker).
rubrics_metrics.description: Tailor your pitch or release to the reporter or editor’s beats, interests, deadlines, and submission preferences so it helps them do their job.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Reporters have assignment areas and personal preferences — read the reporter's past articles and make information useful and appropriate for them. Personalize the pitch to the gatekeeper rather than sending generic blasts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Bust through the clutter.
rubrics_metrics.description: Create a message or pitch that is unusual, unique, and notably interesting to stand out from the large volume of other releases.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A high-impact, distinctive idea can grab a reporter's attention among millions of other releases; aim for something that breaks through rather than blends in.

rubrics_metrics.name: Be timely.
rubrics_metrics.description: Ensure the announcement has news value or a timely angle; if nothing is new, it’s unlikely to be covered.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Timeliness is key — without anything 'new' the item is history. Feature stories may be less urgent but still benefit from a timely hook or angle.

rubrics_metrics.name: Think local first.
rubrics_metrics.description: Emphasize local relevance and how the information matters to people or businesses in the immediate area.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: People relate to nearby news; be clear about how the release is grounded in and meaningful to the local community.

rubrics_metrics.name: Watch your language.
rubrics_metrics.description: Use clear, precise, honest, and straightforward language; avoid jargon, buzzwords, clichés, and overly technical wording.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Editors prefer content that's easy to understand. Avoid vagueness or convoluted phrasing — reporters won't spend time decoding complicated language, even for sophisticated audiences.

rubrics_metrics.name: Have command of your own material.
rubrics_metrics.description: Be prepared to answer reporter questions, know the facts, avoid speculation, and provide access to qualified spokespeople or experts.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Everything is on the record; you may be quoted. Be ready with facts and immediate access to experts or authorities. Don't guess or speculate when responding.

rubrics_metrics.name: Appeal to the heart and the head.
rubrics_metrics.description: Combine emotional/human-interest elements with logical information to make the story meaningful and compelling.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Look for an emotional connection that touches readers and explain how the information helps someone — balance human interest with factual value.

rubrics_metrics.name: A little self-promotion may be too much.
rubrics_metrics.description: Avoid heavy-handed self-promotion, puffery, or exaggeration in PR materials because they turn off newsroom professionals.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: PR should inform and persuade subtly; over-the-top promotion or blatant exaggeration will reduce credibility and interest among editors and reporters.

rubrics_metrics.name: Hold your support materials at the ready.
rubrics_metrics.description: Offer concise initial pitches but have backup materials (data, fact sheets, photos, videos) available and indicate they can be provided on request.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Reporters typically want a brief pitch to start; let them know collateral is available. Know individual editor preferences — sometimes photos or video clips can spark interest and inspire coverage.

rubrics_metrics.name: Proofread what you write (before you send).
rubrics_metrics.description: Eliminate typographical and grammatical errors; have someone else proofread because a single typo can stop an editor from reading further.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: An editor will often not read past the first typographical error. Better yet, get a second set of eyes to proofread your materials before submission.

rubrics_metrics.name: If your first paragraph does not generate interest, all other words will not be read.
rubrics_metrics.description: Lead with a strong, interest-generating first paragraph (lead) because reporters often decide quickly whether to continue reading.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The opening must convey benefit and news value immediately; otherwise the rest of the release is unlikely to be read.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reporters appreciate a personalized "Thank You" for a job well done.
rubrics_metrics.description: Send brief, personalized acknowledgments to reporters after they cover your story to build relationships and show appreciation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A short, tailored thank-you helps foster goodwill and ongoing media relationships; it's a simple courtesy that reporters value.
